subsection: 3. Barring orders under the Domestic Violence Act 2018

notes.h: What the Domestic Violence Act 2018 does (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The Domestic Violence Act 2018 gives people legal protection from domestic violence and abuse. It lets a court make orders that keep an abuser away from the person they are hurting, and in some cases out of the home.
points: The Act came into operation on 1 January 2019 and replaced the earlier domestic violence law with a single, modern code.
Domestic violence under the Act includes physical, sexual and emotional or psychological abuse and threats, so the protection is not limited to physical attacks.
The person who applies for an order is the applicant, and the person the order is made against is the respondent.
Applications are normally made to the District Court, the local court that deals with most family matters.
The court can act urgently, including without the respondent being present, where there is an immediate risk, because waiting for a full hearing could leave the applicant in danger.
Each order is made in response to a specific application, and the court can attach conditions to the order.
notes.tip: Name the Act correctly as the Domestic Violence Act 2018, and name the District Court. For a 10-14 mark question aim for the Act, two or three orders with their effect, and the court.

notes.h: Barring order and who can get one (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The barring order is the order that removes the abuser from the home. Because it affects who may live in a property, it is open to fewer people than the other orders.
points: A barring order requires the respondent to leave the home they share with the applicant (the home the applicant lives in) and to stay away from it.
It lasts for the period the court sets, which is up to three years, and it can be renewed. The court may set a shorter period.
A spouse or civil partner can apply for a barring order, and they do not need to meet the property-interest condition that applies to cohabitants and parents.

A cohabitant (a partner living with the respondent in an intimate relationship) can apply, as can a parent against a respondent of full age who is not a dependent person, such as a non-dependent adult child living in the home.

For cohabitants and parents, the applicant's interest in the home (such as owning or renting it) must not be less than the respondent's. The court cannot make the order if the respondent has an interest and the applicant has none or a lesser one.
This property-interest condition is what keeps barring orders narrower than the other orders.

A barring order protects the applicant, and any dependent children, from further abuse in their own home. It removes the respondent temporarily and does not transfer ownership of the home or end a marriage.
notes.tip: Define a barring order as an order to leave the home and stay away. Do not confuse it with divorce, judicial separation or the Family Home Protection Act, which deal with different things.

notes.h: Safety order and protection order (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Not everyone who needs protection can get a barring order, and not every case needs the respondent removed from the home. Safety and protection orders protect the applicant while the respondent can stay at home.
points: A safety order is a longer-term order that prohibits the respondent from using or threatening violence, from molesting or putting the applicant in fear, and from watching or following them.
A safety order does not remove the respondent from the home, so it suits cases where the applicant only needs protection from violence, threats and following.

Safety orders are open to the widest group, including people who have lived together, parents who have a child together but never lived together, parents against an adult child, and adults living together in a non-contractual relationship such as relatives.
A protection order is a temporary order with the same effect as a safety order, made while an application for a safety order or barring order is waiting to be heard.
A protection order protects the applicant in the meantime, so it can be granted quickly, even before the respondent has been heard.
A protection order is available to anyone who could apply for a safety order or barring order.
notes.tip: Do not define a protection order only as an order that stops threats without making the respondent leave. Say it is temporary and made pending the hearing of the safety or barring order application.

notes.h: Interim and emergency barring orders (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Sometimes the danger is too urgent to wait for a full barring order hearing. Two short-term versions of the barring order deal with these cases.
points: An interim barring order is a short-term barring order made where there is an immediate risk of significant harm to the applicant or a dependent person, and a protection order would not be enough to protect them.
An interim barring order lasts until the application for the full barring order is decided, so it covers the gap before the full hearing.
An emergency barring order is for a person who lived with the respondent but could not get a barring order because they have a lesser interest in the home, or none.
Examples are an unmarried partner without ownership of the home, or a parent of an adult respondent.
The test for harm is the same as for the interim barring order: an immediate risk of significant harm to the applicant or a dependent person.
An emergency barring order lasts a very short period, up to eight working days.
notes.tip: Examiners expect a one-line difference for each order. Say that interim and emergency barring orders are the urgent, short-term versions of the barring order.

notes.b: Five orders can be made under the Act, and the quickest way to keep them apart is to ask two questions: does the respondent have to leave, and is the order urgent or long-term?
points: Safety order: prohibits violence, threats and following; the respondent stays at home, so it is the least disruptive order; longer term.
Protection order: the same protection, but temporary, while a safety order or barring order application waits to be heard.
Barring order: the respondent must leave the home and stay away, for up to three years.
Interim barring order: an urgent, short-term barring order that lasts until the full barring order application is decided.
Emergency barring order: an urgent barring order for a person with a lesser or no interest in the home, lasting up to eight working days.
notes.tip: When asked to name the orders, list safety, protection, barring, interim barring and emergency barring, with a one-line difference for each.

notes.h: Children, criminal penalties and coercive control (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The Act reaches beyond the couple. It protects dependent children, backs its orders with the criminal law and makes controlling behaviour an offence in its own right.
points: The orders can protect the applicant and also a dependent child or other dependent person, so the court can protect a child who lives with the applicant.
Tusla (the Child and Family Agency) can apply on behalf of a person, including a child, in some cases, for a safety or barring order.
Breaking an order is a criminal offence, so the orders are enforced through the criminal law as well as the civil courts.
The Gardaí can arrest a person who breaches an order, and the respondent can be prosecuted.
Coercive control is a criminal offence under the Act. It means knowingly and persistently behaving in a controlling or coercive way towards a partner or former partner, with a serious effect on them.
Examples of coercive control are isolating a person from family and friends, monitoring them, or controlling their money. It applies to people in an intimate or formerly intimate relationship.
notes.tip: Mention that the Act covers coercive control and that breaching an order is a criminal offence. Coercive control is an offence, not an order, so do not list it among the orders.

notes.h: Making and enforcing an application (Higher Level only)
notes.b: The steps are the same whichever order is needed: apply, get urgent help if there is immediate danger, have the case decided, and enforce the order through the Gardaí if it is broken.
points: 1. The applicant applies to the District Court for the relevant order.
2. If there is an immediate risk, the court can make an urgent order, such as a protection order, an interim barring order or an emergency barring order, before the respondent is heard.
3. At the full hearing, the court decides whether to make a safety order or a barring order.
4. If the respondent breaches the order, it is reported to the Gardaí and the breach can be prosecuted.
notes.tip: For an exam answer, give the steps in this order: apply to the District Court, urgent orders can be made quickly, the court decides at the full hearing, and a breach is reported to the Gardaí and prosecuted.

keyTerms.definition: A court order requiring the respondent to leave the shared home and not return for a set period.
A temporary order, made pending the hearing, prohibiting the respondent from molesting or threatening the applicant, without requiring them to leave the home.
A short-term barring order made quickly while the full application is still being considered.
A barring order made where there is an immediate risk of significant harm, lasting a short fixed period.
The person against whom an application for a barring or protection order is made.
A pattern of controlling or coercive behaviour within an intimate relationship, which is a specific offence under the Domestic Violence Act 2018.
A person who lives with another person as a couple without being married or in a civil partnership, and who may apply for orders under the Act.

factCards.term: Orders available under the Domestic Violence Act 2018
factCards.definition: Protection order, interim barring order, emergency barring order and barring order.

factCards.term: Difference between a protection order and a barring order
factCards.definition: A protection order stops the respondent molesting or threatening the applicant; a barring order also requires the respondent to leave the home.
The District Court, which can make interim and emergency orders on an urgent basis.

factCards.term: Consequence of breaching a barring order
factCards.definition: The breach is a criminal offence and can be prosecuted.

questions.prompt: Explain what a barring order under the Domestic Violence Act 2018 requires of the respondent.
questions.model: A barring order requires the respondent to leave the home shared with the applicant and not to return for a set period. It protects the applicant and any dependent children from further abuse in their own home. Breaching the order is a criminal offence.

questions.prompt: Outline the court orders available under the Domestic Violence Act 2018 to protect a person from abuse, and explain when each would be used.
questions.model: A protection order prohibits the respondent from molesting or threatening the applicant but does not require them to leave the home. An interim barring order is a short-term order made quickly while the full application is considered, so that the applicant is protected at once. An emergency barring order is made where there is an immediate risk of significant harm to the applicant or a dependent child, and it lasts for a short fixed period. A barring order is made after the full hearing and requires the respondent to leave the shared home and not return for a set period. Applicants can include a spouse, civil partner, cohabitant, parent of a child or a person in an intimate relationship, and dependent children can be protected. Breach of a barring or protection order is a criminal offence, and coercive control is a specific offence under the Act.
